brief:
Start here, because it changed since last night: you did not train on Saturday, so Pull A never happened — and the deload week starts today, Monday 21 September. That means the Pull A you are walking into is not the one your phone showed you last night. Those 255 lb deadlifts are gone. Everything tonight is deliberately light, and it runs this way through Sunday 27 September. Meso 3, the next hard block, starts Monday 28 September.

Deadlift: 185 for 5, twice. That is it. Your trainers split on this one — the load trainer wanted 200, the recovery trainer wanted 185 — and I took 185. The reason is simple: on 28 August you pulled 235, 255, 265, 265 across four sets; on 10 September, the last time you deadlifted, you pulled 235, 255, 255 across three, a rep short on every set. That is the whole thing sliding backwards at once on the only lift here that can put you on the floor for a week. In a deload being fifteen pounds too light costs you nothing, and being fifteen pounds too heavy costs you the point of the week. Both sets should feel like you could do five more.

Lat pulldown: 66 for 10, two sets. Cable row: 44 in each hand for 10, two sets — and read that as a one-armed dumbbell row, because that is what you actually did in this slot on 10 September and you have still never logged a real cable row at this gym. 44 lb is the 20 kg dumbbell. Curl: 40 for 8, two sets, and 40 means a bar loaded to 40, not 40 lb dumbbells — the 50 you curled on 10 September was a barbell. If you end up with dumbbells, use 25 in each hand. Hammer curls: 27.5 for 10, two sets. Face pulls: 22.5 for 12.

About face pulls, because you should not find this out by surprise. Both trainers argued for keeping both sets — it is the only back-of-the-shoulder work on the day and it has never been what tires you out. The deload rule in the app cuts set counts to about 60%, which on a two-set lift rounds to one, and that rule overrules what I write. So the card may show you one set. Do the second one anyway if you want it; both of your trainers asked for it and I agree with them.

Two things I owe you that I cannot fix from here. First: the Plan screen says this week is "-20% load", and for several lifts that sentence is not true. The app cuts twenty percent and then rounds down to the machine's step, which on the pulldown and the row lands closer to a thirty percent cut. My numbers tonight route around it for Pull A, but every other session this week — Push A, Push B, Legs A, Legs B, Pull B — will still read "-20%" over numbers that are further down than that. I cannot change that sentence; it lives in the plan file and in the code, and I am not allowed to edit either. Second: the plan still calls three of your lifts "Smith" lifts even though you told the app on 2 September that this gym has no smith machine, and you have been running them as barbell lifts. There is no barbell entry in the exercise list to swap them to, so no Yes/No card can fix it. Both of these need a change someone makes in the code, not in a morning review.

Off the gym floor, two numbers that matter more than anything above. Nobody has weighed you since 23 August — 207 lb, 29 days ago — and the show is 161 days out, with the prep block getting written in the assessment week of 2 November. Writing a prep off a blank weight trend is guessing at the one number prep is steered by. Deload week is the cheapest week in the calendar to start weighing again. And your entire log contains one cardio session ever: 15 minutes on an elliptical on 21 July. The plan asks for two to three easy sessions a week during build blocks; Meso 2 ran twenty-eight days and logged none. Meso 3 starts a week today. If conditioning is happening and just not being logged, log it. If it is not happening, that is the biggest gap between here and March.

One Yes/No card is waiting, and it is about Push B, not tonight. Your program trainer wants the side-delt raise back at four sets instead of three. You should know that it is reversing its own cut — it took that lift down to three on 27 August, after you asked on 23 August whether four was really right for such a small muscle. The fact that changed is that the cable raise came off Push A on 11 September, so those three sets are now the only direct side-delt work in your whole week, against seven weekly sets of overhead pressing. That is a real reason and I am passing it to you with its history attached rather than pretending it is a fresh idea.

Every other session this week will still show that sentence over numbers that are further down than it says. Fixing the sentence needs a code or plan change I am not allowed to make.

"DB Curl" 40 means a barbell loaded to 40, not 40 lb dumbbells. The 50 you curled on 10 September was a bar. If you only have dumbbells, use 25 in each hand.

No bodyweight since 23 August — 207 lb, 29 days ago, with the show 161 days out and the prep block being written in the assessment week of 2 November. Deload week is the cheapest week to start weighing again.

Your log holds one cardio session ever: 15 minutes on an elliptical, 21 July. The plan asks for two to three easy sessions a week in build blocks, and Meso 2 logged none in twenty-eight days. Meso 3 starts a week today.

Three of your lifts are still named "Smith" even though you told the app on 2 September that this gym has no smith machine, and you have been doing them with a barbell. No Yes/No card can fix it — the exercise list has no barbell entry to swap to, so it needs a code change.

Your recovery trainer read every note in the log by hand again and found no pain, soreness, tweak or joint complaint anywhere. It reads them by hand because the automatic pain search is still broken — its only hit ever is your 23 August lateral-raise question, matched because "number" contains "numb".

Two logs cannot be read as measurements: on 17 September Legs B has 21 sets stamped inside 23 minutes, and on 10 September two curl sets are stamped 1.3 seconds apart. Those were typed in from memory afterwards. The weights still count; the timing does not.

Three trainers reported. Six disagreements, every one settled by taking one side whole: the recovery trainer won the deadlift, pulldown and row; the load trainer won the curl, hammer curl and face pulls. One advisory fatigue objection, on the deadlift, and I ruled with it. No pain or injury objection from anyone.

proposals.why: The cable lateral raise came off Push A on 11 September, which leaves these three sets as the only direct side-delt work in your whole week, against seven weekly sets of overhead pressing. This asks to put the fourth set back — the same fourth set you ran on 3 August. You should know it reverses itself: your program trainer cut this to three on 27 August, right after you asked whether four was really right for such a small muscle. Those two decisions leaned on each other — August's cut pointed at Push A's cable raises, and September's removal pointed at Push B's dumbbell raises — so the reason for the cut is now gone. Saying yes still leaves you with less side-delt work than you had in August.

overrides.reason: Deload week — 185 for 5, twice, and both sets should feel like five more were there. Your trainers split, 200 against 185, and I took 185: on 28 August you pulled 235/255/265/265 across four sets, and on 10 September you pulled 235/255/255 across three, a rep short on every set. On the one lift that can cost you a week, being light costs nothing.

Two sets of 10 at 66, which is 30 kg — your logged pulls at this gym land on 35, 37.5, 40 and 42.5 kg, so the stack is almost certainly in kilos and 66 is a pin you can actually select. Your load trainer wanted 75; in a deload I take the lighter of the two.

Read this as the one-armed dumbbell row you actually do — that is what you logged here on 10 September, at 55 per hand, and you have never logged a real cable row at this gym. 44 lb is the 20 kg dumbbell, 10 per hand, two sets. If you do find a wide cable row, pick a weight that is a comfortable 10 with three or four left in you and stop there.

40 means the barbell loaded to 40, because the 50 you curled on 10 September was a bar, not dumbbells. Two sets of 8. If you only have dumbbells tonight, use 25 in each hand — your dumbbell curls were 30s and the same fifth comes off those.
27.5 is a fifth off the 35 you have used three sessions running, and two sets instead of three. The app wanted 25, which is nearly a third off and more rest than this lift needs.

Both sets, at 22.5. You have been doing 13 to 15 reps at 27 or 27.5 for weeks without ever being close to failing, so this is not what tires you out, and it is the only back-of-the-shoulder work on the day — in the week your shoulders are meant to be recovering. If the card shows you only one set, that is the app's deload rule trimming it, not me.

dissent.progression: Hold at 200 for 5, twice — that is the app's own 80% of 255 and there is nothing to chase in a deload.
dissent.recovery: Cut to 185 for 5, twice: 10 September went backwards from 28 August on sets, load and reps at once, and this is the lift that can cost a week.
dissent.why: Both seats agreed on two sets and both agreed nothing is being chased tonight, so the whole argument is fifteen pounds. Recovery's regression is real and I checked it: 28 August was 235/255/265/265 over four sets, 10 September was 235/255/255 over three. Recovery also filed the only objection of the morning — advisory, on fatigue, explicitly not on pain, and it said so rather than dressing it up as an injury. Against that, progression's case for 200 is arithmetic, not evidence: it is what 80% rounds to. In the week designed to take work away, on the only lift here that can put him on the floor, fifteen pounds light costs nothing and fifteen pounds heavy costs the point of the week. I also note he had 20 September completely off and has not deadlifted in eleven days — which cuts toward progression, and still does not outweigh a load that only has downside.

dissent.progression: Push to 75 — a true 20% off the 93 he pulled here, because the app's 67.5 is nearer a 28% cut.
dissent.recovery: Cut to 66, which is 30 kg and an actual selectable pin, rather than 70 or 75 which are not.
dissent.why: This is the ladder's own case: progression says push, recovery says cut, and it is a deload week, so the lower load wins and I do not get to weigh it. It is also the better number on its merits. Recovery's kilo reading holds up when I check it — 77, 83, 88 and 93 lb are 34.9, 37.6, 39.9 and 42.2 kg, which is 35 / 37.5 / 40 / 42.5 to within a rounding error. Progression's 75 is a number that may not exist on the machine.

dissent.progression: 45 per hand for 10, two sets, keeping the dumbbell.
dissent.recovery: 44 per hand for 10, two sets — 44 lb is the 20 kg dumbbell he already used on 15 September.
dissent.why: One pound apart, and both seats independently reached the same conclusion that matters: this slot is a one-armed dumbbell row and should be priced as one. I took 44 because it is a dumbbell that demonstrably exists on his rack — he logged 20 kg on 15 September — where 45 is a guess at an imperial rack in a gym whose weights keep coming out as round kilos. Deload week, lower of the two, and it is the one with a receipt.

Same bar, same two sets; the only argument is two reps. Neither seat put a fatigue case behind it — recovery's own note on this lift is about data quality, not tiredness. In the week whose job is to take work away I take the smaller number, and 8 is the bottom of the slot's own 8-to-10 range, which is where a deload belongs.

Identical weight — both seats independently landed on a fifth off the 35 he has used three sessions running, which is as close to agreement as this panel gets. One rep apart, and for the same reason as the curl I take the lighter side: 10 is the bottom of the slot's 10-to-12 range.

dissent.progression: Keep both sets, drop the weight to 22.5 for 12.
dissent.recovery: Keep both sets at the full 27.5 for 13 — no cut at all on the only shoulder-health work of the day.
dissent.why: The seats agree on the thing that actually matters, which is that two sets survive; they differ only on whether the weight comes down with everything else. Progression says push, recovery says hold, it is a deload week, so the ladder hands it to the lower load and I agree with the ladder here — a deload that exempts a lift because it is easy is a deload with a hole in it, and 22.5 for 12 is still every bit of the shoulder work the set is there to do. I am recording separately that the app's own set budget may cut this to one set regardless of what either trainer or I asked for, and he is told that in plain words rather than discovering it on the card.
